questions.q: Name the single most effective first-aid step for a fresh blood stain on wool and explain why hot water must be avoided.
questions.a: Correct: Flush immediately with cold water, then apply a neutral-pH enzymatic detergent. Hot water coagulates the protein (haemoglobin), setting the stain permanently. A wrong answer (e.g., "soak in hot soapy water") reveals the student confuses protein stains with grease stains and ignores fibre damage.

questions.q: A student treats a tea stain on silk with sodium hypochlorite bleach. The stain lightens but the fabric yellows and weakens. Explain the chemical reason for the damage and name a safe alternative oxidising agent for silk.
questions.a: Correct: Hypochlorite (high pH, strong oxidiser) hydrolyses silk's peptide bonds and oxidises residual sericin to yellow chromophores. Safe alternative: hydrogen peroxide (3 %) at pH 7–8 with a short contact time. A wrong answer shows the student does not link fibre chemistry (protein fibre = acid-stable, alkali-labile) to bleach selection.

questions.q: You have a ballpoint ink stain on polyester. Design a 4-step removal sequence using only household reagents, justifying each step's chemical action.
questions.a: Correct sequence: (1) Blot with dry cloth — mechanical removal of excess dye/solvent. (2) Sponge with isopropyl alcohol (70 %) — dissolves the dye carrier (glycol) and resin binder. (3) Apply liquid dish-wash detergent + warm water — emulsifies residual oil. (4) Rinse, then air-dry. A wrong sequence (e.g., starting with hot water) spreads the dye and sets the resin.

questions.q: Compare the removal of turmeric (curry) stain from cotton versus wool. Why is lemon juice (citric acid) recommended for cotton but contra-indicated for wool?
questions.a: Correct: Turmeric's curcumin is a pH-sensitive dye; acid (lemon) converts it to a colourless form on cotton (cellulose tolerates pH 3–4). Wool's amide linkages hydrolyse below pH 5, causing fibre damage. For wool, use glycerine + lukewarm water to solubilise the oily carrier, then mild detergent. A wrong answer misses the fibre-pH stability difference.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Enzyme pre-soak works equally well for all protein stains (blood, egg, milk, perspiration) on all fabrics." Defend or refute with three specific exceptions.
questions.a: Correct: Refute. (1) Perspiration contains urea/lactic acid — enzyme works but alkalinity from sweat can inactivate protease; pre-rinse needed. (2) Silk/wool are protein fibres — protease digests the fabric itself; use non-enzymatic detergent. (3) Old, heat-set blood cross-links — enzyme cannot penetrate; needs oxidising bleach first. A wrong evaluation shows over-generalisation without considering fibre chemistry or stain age.

questions.q: Create a stain-removal decision flowchart (text-based) that a Class 12 student could use for any unknown stain on an unknown fabric. Include at least four decision nodes (e.g., stain class, fibre type, colourfastness, reagent availability).
questions.a: Good answer: START → Is stain fresh? YES → Blot/rinse cold water. NO → Identify class (protein/tannin/oil/dye/mineral) via simple tests (solubility, smell, colour). → Identify fibre (burn test/label). → Test colourfastness on seam. → Select reagent ladder per table. → Apply mildest first, escalate. → Rinse, dry. Poor answer omits colourfastness test or treats all fibres identically.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you spill ______-laden curry on a white cotton kurta and a silk dupatta simultaneously.

questions.a: Specific stain removal methods are targeted procedures using chemical reagents (solvents, enzymes, bleaches, acids/alkalis) and physical techniques (sponging, blotting, soaking) to dissolve, emulsify, or break down the staining substance without damaging the fabric, selected based on the stain's chemical nature (protein, tannin, oil.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Specific stain removal methods?
questions.a: Students think "bleach removes all coloured stains" and use chlorine bleach on coloured cotton, silk, or wool.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can look at an unknown stain on a given fabric, identify its probable class (protein/tannin/grease/dye/mineral), select the correct reagent sequence (e.g., cold water → enzyme → oxidising bleach for blood on cotton), and justify each step with the underlying chemical principle.
